_README: Deliberate shrinkages, so that check 17 can tell one from data loss (#1143).
verify_release.py check 17 fails a release where an artifact lost more than
DROP_THRESHOLD of its bytes against the previous release, and it is right to:
a POI file that halved is usually a build that lost half its data. But this
project deliberately shrinks artifacts - a gate that culls unreachable water,
an exporter that stops publishing roads as resupply, a basemap that drops
layers nothing draws - and until this file existed there was NO WAY TO SAY SO.
The check's only exemption is an upstream that changed, which a pipeline cull
is not. So the gate went red, stayed red, and the verdict lived nowhere.
THE COST OF HAVING NO ANSWER, measured rather than argued. `Verify release`
has failed 8 of its 9 runs ever. Its 2026-08-26 run against production failed
five checks, every one of them a cull somebody had decided on purpose:
poi_water     -65%  osm_water 1,535 -> 201 points. #749's reachability gate
reaching production at last; #916 recorded the exact
1,535 ungated points the bucket was serving. Measured
2026-08-28 by counting features in both release folders:
every other water source held or grew (atc_csi 138->145).
poi_resupply  -47%  opentrail_at 72 -> 0. #824, 'r is not resupply: stop
publishing 72 roads and gaps as places to buy food'.
atc_communities unchanged at 59. The 72 matches exactly.
trails        -13%  centerline 3,025 -> 461 FEATURES and 251,620 -> 249,038
VERTICES. Merged centerline chains (#835): a sixth as
many features carrying the same geometry, so the bytes
lost are repeated per-feature property blocks. Nothing
about the trail moved.
None of those three is an entry below, and that is the mechanism working
rather than a gap in it: three more releases have been published since, so
2026-08-18 is no longer any release's predecessor and the comparison that
failed no longer happens. AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT IS ONLY EVER ABOUT ONE PAIR OF
RELEASES, and that is what stops this file becoming a place where checks go
to die. `from_release` names the predecessor the drop is measured against;
the moment a newer release takes that place, the entry is inert. Nobody has
to remember to delete it, and nothing is silenced a second time by accident.
`max_drop` is the other half. An acknowledgement is a ceiling, not a blanket:
a drop past it fails exactly as before, and says that an acknowledgement
exists and does not cover this much. Acknowledging 'water will shrink by
about two thirds' must not also acknowledge water vanishing.
WHAT AN ENTRY OWES ITS READER, and the reason this file is in reference/
rather than in code: every row is somebody's decision that a specific
shrinkage is intended, and reviewing a diff of this file reviews those
decisions. So a row carries the artifact, the predecessor, the ceiling, WHO
decided (the issue or pull request that shipped the change), and the
measurement that establishes it is not data loss. A row without evidence is
a row that turns a safety gate off on somebody's say-so.
An artifact may be a `*` pattern, and exactly one row uses it: the 44
per-stretch basemap cuts come off one build through one extract, so they are
one decision. Forty-four identical rows would be less reviewable rather than
more - the thing this directory's line ceiling exists to prevent - and a
pattern that ever covers two decisions should be split back into rows.
check_output_quality.py's `flag_drops()` is the build-time version of this
same check and has the same blind spot. It is not wired to this file: its
baseline is a gitignored local file that is absent on a hosted runner, so it
reports SKIPPED in CI anyway. Worth doing together with #1026 if that ever
changes.
